Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M,E,P$ have exactly the compact, boundaryless, scalar-positive-symbol and formal symmetry hypotheses of [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]], with $\operatorname{dom}P=H^2(M,E)$. Write $\mathcal H=\ker P$.

Then $\mathcal H$ is finite dimensional and consists of smooth sections, $\operatorname{ran}P=\mathcal H^\perp$ is closed in $L^2$, and
$$L^2(M,E)=\mathcal H\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\operatorname{ran}P.$$
Let $\Pi$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal H$. There is a unique linear operator $G:L^2\to H^2\cap\mathcal H^\perp$ with
$$PG=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }L^2,\qquad GP=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }H^2,\qquad G\Pi=\Pi G=0.$$
It is bounded from $H^k$ to $H^{k+2}$ for every integer $k\ge0$, compact and selfadjoint on $L^2$, and preserves smooth sections. For all such $k$,
$$H^k=\mathcal H\oplus P(H^{k+2}),\qquad C^\infty(M,E)=\mathcal H\oplus P(C^\infty(M,E)),$$
where the second summands are the corresponding intersections with $\mathcal H^\perp$, and the decompositions are topological. The projection is smoothing: for every integer $r\ge0$, $\|\Pi f\|_{C^r}\le C_r\|f\|_2$. Consequently $G$ is a two-sided parametrix with finite-rank smoothing remainders. If additionally $(Pu,u)_2\ge0$ for smooth $u$, then $P$ and $G$ are nonnegative on their respective domains.

Let $(U,x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ be a smooth chart on a smooth manifold and
$\omega$ a smooth $k$-form on $U$, with $k\ge0$. Summing over increasing
$k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$
For every differential form $\omega$, $d(d\omega)=0$.

The real **de Rham cohomology** is $H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)=Z^k(M)/B^k(M)$, with $Z^k,B^k$ as in [[def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms]].

This is [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]] in real vector spaces. Only a closed form $\omega$ represents a class $[\omega]$. For closed forms $\omega,\omega\prime$, equality $[\omega]=[\omega\prime]$ means precisely $\omega\prime-\omega=d\eta$ for some $(k-1)$-form $\eta$. Addition and real scalar multiplication are induced by those of forms. All groups on the empty manifold are zero.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be open. Write $\Omega^k(U;\mathbb C)$ for smooth
complex-valued $k$-forms. For increasing multi-indices
$I=(i_1<\cdots<i_p)$ and $J=(j_1<\cdots<j_q)$, write
$dz^I=dz_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dz_{i_p}$ and
$d\bar z^J=d\bar z_{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge d\bar z_{j_q}$. The invertible
change of cotangent basis
$dz_j=dx_j+i\,dy_j$, $d\bar z_j=dx_j-i\,dy_j$ gives the direct sum
decomposition

$$\Omega^k(U;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\Omega^{p,q}(U),\qquad \Omega^{p,q}(U)=\left\{\sum_{I,J}a_{I,J}(z)\,dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J:a_{I,J}\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb C)\right\},$$

where $0\le p,q\le n$ and every sum is finite. On a $(p,q)$ form
$\eta=\sum_{I,J}a_{I,J}dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J$, define

$$\partial\eta=\sum_{I,J,j}(\partial_{z_j}a_{I,J})\,dz_j\wedge dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J,\qquad \bar\partial\eta=\sum_{I,J,j}(\partial_{\bar z_j}a_{I,J})\,d\bar z_j\wedge dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J.$$

Repeated differentials vanish by alternation; components outside the range
$0\le p,q\le n$ are zero. These operators are the components of $d$ of
bidegrees $(p+1,q)$ and $(p,q+1)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be open and let all forms below be smooth and
complex-valued. Then
$$d=\partial+\bar\partial,\qquad \partial^2=0,\qquad \bar\partial^2=0,\qquad \partial\bar\partial+\bar\partial\partial=0.$$
For $\eta\in\Omega^{p,q}(U)$ and $\theta\in\Omega^{r,s}(U)$,
$$\partial(\eta\wedge\theta)=\partial\eta\wedge\theta+(-1)^{p+q}\eta\wedge\partial\theta,\qquad \bar\partial(\eta\wedge\theta)=\bar\partial\eta\wedge\theta+(-1)^{p+q}\eta\wedge\bar\partial\theta.$$
The identities hold at bidegree endpoints as well, with components outside
$0\le p,q\le n$ interpreted as zero.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for density integration and
completion. Let $X$ be a complex manifold of dimension $m\ge1$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]) with a Hermitian
metric $g$, and let $E\to X$ be a holomorphic vector bundle of rank $r$ with a
Hermitian metric $h$ ([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]).
Fix integers $p,q\ge0$. In a holomorphic chart with coordinates
$z=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)$ and a holomorphic frame of $E$, an **$E$-valued
$(p,q)$-form** is an expression
$$s=\sum_{|I|=p}\sum_{|J|=q}s_{IJ}\otimes dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J,$$
with $s_{IJ}$ smooth local sections of $E$ and increasing multi-indices $I,J$
([[def-bigraded-complex-differential-forms]]); such expressions agree on
overlaps because holomorphic changes of coordinates preserve bidegree and
holomorphic frame changes are complex-linear. The resulting smooth global
sections of the bundle $\Lambda^{p,q}T^*X\otimes E$ are denoted
$\mathcal A^{p,q}(X,E)$; the bundle is zero, and so is
$\mathcal A^{p,q}(X,E)$, when $p>m$ or $q>m$.

The **Dolbeault operator** is the first-order operator
$$\bar\partial_E:\mathcal A^{p,q}(X,E)\to\mathcal A^{p,q+1}(X,E),\qquad \bar\partial_E s=\sum_{I,J}\sum_{k=1}^m \bar\partial_{z_k}s_{IJ}\otimes d\bar z_k\wedge dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J,$$
with the Wirtinger operators $\bar\partial_{z_k}$
([[def-wirtinger-operators-in-several-complex-variables]],
[[def-bigraded-complex-differential-forms]]) acting componentwise on the local
sections $s_{IJ}$. It is independent of the holomorphic chart and frame, and
$\bar\partial_E^2=0$
([[thm-d-dbar-decomposition-and-identities]]); both assertions are proved
below.

Equip $\Lambda^{p,q}T^*X\otimes E$ with the Hermitian metric induced by $g$ and
$h$ ([[prop-riemannian-metrics-induce-metrics-on-dual-tensor-and-exterior-bundles]]
and [[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]). For compactly
supported smooth $s,t\in\mathcal A^{p,q}(X,E)$ the **$L^2$ pairing**
$$\langle s,t\rangle_{L^2}=\int_X\langle s,t\rangle\,d\mu_g$$
uses the Riemannian volume density $\mu_g$
([[def-riemannian-volume-density]],
[[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-smooth-density]]) and is a complex
inner product in the first-variable-linear convention
([[def-complex-l-two-inner-product]]); its completion
$L^2(X,\Lambda^{p,q}T^*X\otimes E)$ is a complex Hilbert space
by the completion argument below, using
[[thm-metric-completion-carries-a-unique-banach-space-structure]]. By
[[lem-formal-adjoints-of-differential-operators-exist-and-are-unique]] the
operator $\bar\partial_E$ has a **formal adjoint**
$\bar\partial_E^*:\mathcal A^{p,q+1}(X,E)\to\mathcal A^{p,q}(X,E)$, the unique
smooth first-order operator with
$$\langle\bar\partial_Es,t\rangle_{L^2}=\langle s,\bar\partial_E^*t\rangle_{L^2}$$
for all compactly supported smooth forms.

The **Dolbeault Laplacian**
$\Delta_{\bar\partial_E}=\bar\partial_E\bar\partial_E^*+\bar\partial_E^*\bar\partial_E$
is a formally symmetric Laplace-type second-order operator
([[def-second-order-laplace-type-operators-on-vector-bundles]]) preserving each
bidegree $(p,q)$, with
$$\langle\Delta_{\bar\partial_E}s,s\rangle_{L^2}=\|\bar\partial_Es\|_2^2+\|\bar\partial_E^*s\|_2^2\ge0$$
for compactly supported smooth $s$. Its principal symbol is
$\sigma_2(\Delta_{\bar\partial_E})(x,\xi)=|\xi^{0,1}|_g^2\,\mathrm{id}$, where
$\xi^{0,1}$ is the $(0,1)$-part of $\xi\in T_x^*X$; in particular the principal
form is smooth, and it is positive definite on nonzero real covectors.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the density-integral
convention. Let $M$ be a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold without boundary,
$\mu$ a smooth positive density on $M$, and $E,F\to M$ finite-rank smooth vector
bundles over $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ with smooth bundle metrics,
Hermitian (first-variable-linear) in the complex case, with the conventions of
[[def-second-order-laplace-type-operators-on-vector-bundles]]. Let
$P:\Gamma(E)\to\Gamma(F)$ be a linear differential operator of order at most two
(the target-$F$ version of the local description in
[[def-second-order-laplace-type-operators-on-vector-bundles]]).

Then there is a unique linear differential operator $P^\star:\Gamma(F)\to\Gamma(E)$
of order at most two such that
$$\int_M\langle Pu,v\rangle_F\,d\mu=\int_M\langle u,P^\star v\rangle_E\,d\mu$$
for all compactly supported smooth sections $u\in\Gamma_c(E)$ and
$v\in\Gamma_c(F)$; it is the **formal adjoint** of $P$. It is given locally as
follows: in a chart with coordinates $x$, with density coefficient $\gamma>0$
defined by $\mu=\gamma\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$
([[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]), with frames of $E$ and $F$
orthonormal for the metrics (equivalently unitary in the complex case; such
frames exist locally by applying Gram–Schmidt to any local frame,
[[thm-gram-schmidt-orthonormalisation]]), and with local coefficients
$Pu=\sum_{|\alpha|\le2}a_\alpha D^\alpha u$,
$$P^\star v=\sum_{|\alpha|\le2}(-1)^{|\alpha|}\gamma^{-1}D^\alpha\bigl(\gamma\,a_\alpha^*v\bigr),$$
where $a_\alpha^*$ is the fibre adjoint. Consequently:
1. if the leading coefficients of $P$ of order $\delta\in\{0,1,2\}$ are the
   matrices $a_\alpha$, $|\alpha|=\delta$, then those of $P^\star$ are
   $(-1)^\delta a_\alpha^*$, computed in the same orthonormal frames; in
   particular the formal adjoint of a Laplace-type operator is again Laplace
   type and its principal symbol is unchanged,
   $\sigma_2(P^\star)=\sigma_2(P)$;
2. $(P^\star)^\star=P$;
3. if $E=F$, then $P$ is formally symmetric in the sense of
   [[def-second-order-laplace-type-operators-on-vector-bundles]] exactly when
   $P=P^\star$.

Let $M$ be a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold without boundary of
dimension $n\ge2$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]), let $\mu$ be a smooth positive
density on $M$ ([[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]), and let $E\to M$ be
a finite-rank smooth vector bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-bundle-rank-fibre-and-trivial-bundle]]) over
$\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ carrying a smooth bundle metric
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ ([[def-smooth-bundle-metric]]), Euclidean in the
real case and Hermitian, linear in the first variable, in the complex case; in
the complex case the fibres are complex vector spaces through a smooth complex
structure on $E$
([[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]]). Write $\Gamma(E)$
for the smooth sections ([[def-smooth-section-local-section-and-support]]).

A $\mathbb K$-linear map $P:\Gamma(E)\to\Gamma(E)$ is a **linear differential
operator of order at most two** on $E$ when, on every chart domain $\Omega$ of
$M$ with coordinates $x=(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ and in every local frame of $E$ over
$\Omega$ in which a section is written $s\leftrightarrow u=(u^1,\ldots,u^r)$
and its image as $Ps\leftrightarrow((Ps)_1,\ldots,(Ps)_r)$,
$$(Ps)_\lambda=-\sum_{i,j=1}^na^{ij}_{\lambda\mu}(x)\,\partial_i\partial_ju^\mu(x)+\sum_{j=1}^nb^j_{\lambda\mu}(x)\,\partial_ju^\mu(x)+c_{\lambda\mu}(x)u^\mu(x),\qquad1\le\lambda\le r,$$
with smooth coefficient functions on $\Omega$ and summation over the repeated
index $\mu$ (and over $i,j$). Such an operator is **Laplace type** when in
addition, in every such chart and frame, its second-order coefficients are
scalar multiples of the identity, $a^{ij}_{\lambda\mu}=a^{ij}\delta_{\lambda\mu}$,
with $a^{ij}$ smooth real functions for which the matrix $(a^{ij}(x))$ is
symmetric and positive definite at every $x\in\Omega$. Its **principal symbol**
is the endomorphism-valued quadratic function
$\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)=a^{ij}(x)\xi_i\xi_j\,\mathrm{id}_{E_x}$ for
$\xi\in T_x^*M$. Its scalar principal form $a$ is a smooth section of
$\mathrm{Sym}^2TM$ ([[def-smooth-tensor-field]]), since it acts on two
covectors, and $a_x(\xi,\xi)>0$ for $\xi\ne0$. For positive-rank $E$ the
symbol determines $a$ uniquely. On the zero-rank bundle the operator and its
symbol are zero; a supplied smooth positive-definite form $a$ is part of the
Laplace-type data in this degenerate case.

For the density-integral convention assume Countable Choice
([[def-countable-choice]]). $P$ is **formally symmetric** for
$(\mu,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ when
$$\int_M\langle Ps,t\rangle\,d\mu=\int_M\langle s,Pt\rangle\,d\mu$$
for all compactly supported smooth sections $s,t\in\Gamma_c(E)$
([[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-smooth-density]]).

**Well-definedness.** The definition is local. On a fixed chart and frame the
displayed assignment is a $\mathbb K$-linear map on components with smooth
coefficients, and the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]])
computes the transition to another chart and frame on the overlap: the
second-order coefficients transform by the symmetric tensor rule
$a'^{kl}=a^{ij}\frac{\partial x'^k}{\partial x^i}\frac{\partial x'^l}{\partial x^j}$
together with conjugation by the frame-change matrix, while the terms produced
by the second derivatives of the coordinate change are absorbed into the
first-order coefficients. Hence a single operator that admits a local
expression on one cover admits a local expression on every chart and frame, and
the two hypotheses placed on the leading coefficient are invariant: scalar-ness
is preserved by frame conjugation and by the coordinate rule for a field of
symmetric matrices, and symmetric positive definiteness is preserved by both.
For positive rank the scalar principal form, and in every rank the principal
symbol, are therefore independent of the chart and frame, since two
local expressions of the same operator differ by an operator of order at most
one; the symbol is smooth in $(x,\xi)$ because the $a^{ij}$ are smooth, and
the scalar principal form is positive on nonzero covectors exactly when
$(a^{ij})$ is positive definite.
Formal symmetry is an identity between integrals of compactly supported smooth
sections and therefore depends only on the operator, the density and the
metric.

A Riemannian metric induces smooth metrics on dual, tensor and exterior bundles. On decomposable covectors, $\langle\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k,\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_k\rangle=\det(\langle\alpha_i,\beta_j\rangle)$; increasing orthonormal wedge monomials have norm one.

The **Riemannian volume density** is $\mu_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in coordinates.

The matrix is that of [[prop-coordinate-criterion-for-a-riemannian-metric]], so its determinant is positive and smooth. The density frames and their absolute-Jacobian law are [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]. In dimension zero take the empty determinant to be one, giving weight one at every point, independently of orientation. The compatibility of these local formulas is proved in [[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]].

For a smooth manifold $M^n$, with boundary allowed, the **density bundle** is $DM=\coprod_{p\in M}D(T_pM)$. In coordinates $x$, let $|dx|=|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ be the density taking value one on the coordinate frame. On overlaps,
$$|dy|=|\det D_x y|\,|dx|.$$
A smooth density is a section with smooth real coefficient in these frames. Its support is the closure of its nonzero locus. The absolute determinants are positive smooth transition functions and satisfy the cocycle identities by the chain rule. A countable atlas and [[thm-vector-bundle-construction-from-a-smooth-cocycle]] therefore give a smooth line bundle. For boundary charts the same gluing proof uses half-space product charts; smoothness of transitions follows from their local extensions, and Hausdorffness and second countability follow as for the supplied cocycle construction. The fibers are lines by [[prop-one-densities-form-a-one-dimensional-vector-space]]. When $n=0$ the empty frame trivializes $DM=M\times\mathbb R$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $\delta$ be a compactly supported smooth density on $M^n$, with boundary allowed. Choose a chart partition $(\rho_i)$ and write $\rho_i\delta=f_i|dx_i|$. For $n\geq1$ define
$$\int_M\delta=\sum_i\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widetilde f_i(x_i)\,dx_i.$$
The zero extensions are Riemann integrable, including at genuine faces, by [[lem-chart-supported-coefficients-have-well-defined-riemann-integrable-half-space-extensions]]. The compact-support/local-finiteness argument of [[lem-a-locally-finite-sum-is-finite-near-the-compact-support-of-a-form]] applies to density supports as closed sets, so the sum is finite. For $n=0$ sum the scalar density values over the finite support, without orientation signs. Empty support gives zero. Choice independence is discharged by [[thm-density-integration-is-defined-without-an-orientation]].

Let $m\ge1$. A **chart** on a topological space $X$ is a homeomorphism
$\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ from an open set $U\subseteq X$ onto an open subset of
$\mathbb C^m$ with its usual topology ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]);
two charts $\varphi,\psi$ are **holomorphically compatible** when the
transition maps $\psi\circ\varphi^{-1}$ and $\varphi\circ\psi^{-1}$ are
holomorphic on the open sets where they are defined
([[def-holomorphic-function-in-several-complex-variables]]). A **holomorphic
atlas** is a family of pairwise compatible charts whose domains cover $X$. A
**complex manifold of dimension $m$** is a nonempty Hausdorff
([[def-hausdorff-space]]) second-countable ([[def-second-countable-space]])
topological space carrying a holomorphic atlas; the same maximal-atlas argument
as for [[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]] applies verbatim with
$\mathbb C^m$ in place of $\mathbb C$: the union of a holomorphic atlas with all
charts compatible with it is again a holomorphic atlas, so one passes to the
unique maximal atlas and calls its members holomorphic charts. Each chart is a
homeomorphism onto an open subset of $\mathbb C^m\cong\mathbb R^{2m}$, so $X$ is
a topological manifold without boundary of real dimension $2m$
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]), and for connected $X$ the case
$m=1$ recovers Riemann surfaces ([[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]]).

A **holomorphic map** $f:X\to Y$ between complex manifolds is a continuous map
whose expression in every pair of holomorphic charts is holomorphic
([[def-holomorphic-map-and-complex-jacobian]]); equivalently, for every open
$V\subseteq Y$ and every holomorphic function $h$ on $V$, the function
$h\circ f$ is holomorphic on $f^{-1}(V)$. The forward implication is the
holomorphic chain rule; conversely apply this condition to the coordinate
functions of a chart on $Y$.

**Induced smooth structure and complex structure.** Holomorphic functions on
open subsets of $\mathbb C^m$ are smooth
([[cor-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables-are-smooth]]), so every
holomorphic atlas is a smooth atlas ([[def-smooth-atlas]]) and $X$ is a smooth
manifold of real dimension $2m$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]) whose smooth charts
include the holomorphic ones. In holomorphic coordinates
$z_k=x_k+iy_k$ the **complex structure** is the endomorphism field $J$ of the
tangent bundle determined by $J\partial_{x_k}=\partial_{y_k}$ and
$J\partial_{y_k}=-\partial_{x_k}$; it satisfies $J^2=-\mathrm{id}$ and is
independent of the holomorphic chart, because a holomorphic transition map has
complex-linear differential ([[def-holomorphic-map-and-complex-jacobian]],
[[thm-chain-rule-for-holomorphic-maps-in-several-variables]]) and complex-linear
maps intertwine the two coordinate definitions of multiplication by $i$. A
**Hermitian metric** on $X$ is a Riemannian metric $g$
([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]) satisfying
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all tangent vectors $v,w$; its Riemannian volume density
is written $\mu_g$ ([[def-riemannian-volume-density]]). The complex structure
makes each tangent space a complex vector space, so the tangent bundle is a
smooth complex vector bundle in the sense of
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]].

**Holomorphic vector bundles and Hermitian bundle metrics.** A **holomorphic
vector bundle of rank $r$** on $X$ is a smooth complex vector bundle
$\pi:E\to X$ of rank $r$
([[def-smooth-vector-bundle-rank-fibre-and-trivial-bundle]],
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]]) together with an open
cover $(V_\alpha)$ of $X$ and smooth local trivializations
$\theta_\alpha:E|_{V_\alpha}\to V_\alpha\times\mathbb C^r$ whose transition
matrices $g_{\alpha\beta}:V_\alpha\cap V_\beta\to\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathbb C)$,
defined by $\theta_\alpha\theta_\beta^{-1}(p,v)=(p,g_{\alpha\beta}(p)v)$, are
holomorphic. A **holomorphic frame** over an open set $V$ is a smooth
complex-linear trivialization whose transition matrices with the supplied
trivializations are holomorphic on every overlap. Changing holomorphic frame multiplies a local section by a
holomorphic matrix, hence a smooth local section is **holomorphic** exactly when
its representatives in holomorphic frames are holomorphic functions. A
**Hermitian metric** $h$ on $E$ is a smooth bundle metric
([[def-smooth-bundle-metric]]) whose fibre pairings are positive definite
Hermitian forms, linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the
second; the condition is frame-independent because the gauge freedom is
conjugation by a pointwise invertible matrix. Smooth sections are
$\Gamma(E)$ ([[def-smooth-section-local-section-and-support]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

A Riemannian metric induces smooth metrics on dual, tensor and exterior bundles. On decomposable covectors, $\langle\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k,\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_k\rangle=\det(\langle\alpha_i,\beta_j\rangle)$; increasing orthonormal wedge monomials have norm one.

derivations.claim: The de Rham Laplacian satisfies the hypotheses of [F1]. Let $D=d$ on real forms, or on their complexification, and $P=DD^*+D^*D$. The coordinate formula [F2] exhibits $D$ as a smooth first-order differential operator, so [F4] supplies its unique smooth first-order formal adjoint $D^*$. In an orthonormal basis of the cotangent space at a point ([F7]), the leading coefficient matrices of $D$ multiply, on a covector $\xi$, to exterior multiplication $\varepsilon(\xi)$, and those of $D^*$ are $(-1)^1$ times the metric adjoints, so they multiply to $-\varepsilon(\xi)^*$. The coefficient of $\partial_i\partial_j$ in $DD^*$ is therefore $\varepsilon(\xi)\bigl(-\varepsilon(\xi)^*\bigr)$ and in $D^*D$ it is $\bigl(-\varepsilon(\xi)^*\bigr)\varepsilon(\xi)$; by [F5] the second-order coefficient matrix of $P$ is $-(\varepsilon(\xi)\varepsilon(\xi)^*+\varepsilon(\xi)^*\varepsilon(\xi))$. The metric adjoint of $\varepsilon(\xi)$ is the contraction that deletes each factor of a wedge monomial pairing with $\xi$, with alternating signs, and deleting and reinserting the same factor on both sides gives the identity $\varepsilon(\xi)\varepsilon(\xi)^*+\varepsilon(\xi)^*\varepsilon(\xi)=|\xi|^2\mathrm{id}$; hence the second-order coefficient of $P$ is $-|\xi|^2\mathrm{id}$ and its principal symbol in the sense of [F5] is $\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)=|\xi|^2\mathrm{id}$, a smooth positive definite scalar form. Finally, for compactly supported smooth forms, $(Pu,v)_{L^2}=(D^*u,D^*v)_{L^2}+(Du,Dv)_{L^2}$ by [F4], which is conjugate-symmetric in $u,v$ and equals $\|Du\|_2^2+\|D^*u\|_2^2\ge0$ when $u=v$; so $P$ is formally symmetric and nonnegative. Thus [F1] applies to $P$ with domain $H^2$.

The Dolbeault Laplacian satisfies the hypotheses of [F1]. Fix $p$ and let $D=\bar\partial_E$ on the sum over $q$, $P=DD^*+D^*D$, with the operator and its adjoint as in [F3]; by that item $D$ is a smooth first-order operator and the Dolbeault Laplacian is the formally symmetric Laplace-type operator with $\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)=|\xi^{0,1}|^2\mathrm{id}$, notation as in [F5]. The same computation as in step 1.1, now with $\eta=\xi^{0,1}$ and unitary frames ([F7]), gives the deletion identity $\varepsilon(\eta)\varepsilon(\eta)^*+\varepsilon(\eta)^*\varepsilon(\eta)=|\eta|^2\mathrm{id}$ including the holomorphic $p$-factors and the bundle factor, so the second-order coefficient is $-|\eta|^2\mathrm{id}$ and the principal symbol is $|\xi^{0,1}|^2\mathrm{id}$; for a nonzero real covector the $(0,1)$-part is nonzero, so the form is positive definite. The energy identity and formal symmetry are those established in [F3], and no K\"ahler hypothesis is used. Hence [F1] applies to this $P$ as well.

Consequences of $D^2=0$. Squaring $D^2=0$ and transposing the adjoint identity gives $(D^*)^2=0$, and expanding the two products gives $PD=DP$ and $PD^*=D^*P$. On smooth forms the energy identity of steps 1.1 and 2.1 shows $Pu=0$ exactly when $Du=0$ and $D^*u=0$; [F1] makes every $L^2$-harmonic element smooth, so this describes $\ker P$ on $H^2$ as well. Harmonic forms are orthogonal to the images of $D$ and $D^*$: for harmonic $h$, $(Dv,h)_{L^2}=(v,D^*h)_{L^2}=0$ and $(D^*v,h)_{L^2}=(v,Dh)_{L^2}=0$. Since $D$ raises the degree by one in the de Rham grading and the second bidegree by one in the Dolbeault bigrading, while $D^*$ lowers it, the operator $P$ preserves degrees, and the unique orthogonal solution defining $G$ in [F1] preserves degree: its other degree components solve the homogeneous equation and lie in the orthogonal complement of the kernel, hence vanish; the harmonic projection preserves degree as well.

Commutation identities. For smooth $u$, $P(DGu)=D(PGu)=D(u-\Pi u)=Du$ by step 3.1 and [F1]. The section $DGu$ is smooth and orthogonal to $\ker P$ by step 3.1, and $Du$ is orthogonal to $\ker P$ as well; by the uniqueness of the orthogonal solution in [F1], $DGu=GDu$. The same reasoning applied to $D^*$ gives $D^*G=GD^*$. Since $\Pi$ projects onto $\ker P$ and the images of $D$ and $D^*$ are orthogonal to it, $D\Pi=D^*\Pi=0$; taking adjoints and using that $\Pi$ is an orthogonal projection gives $\Pi D=\Pi D^*=0$. All identities are asserted on smooth forms, so no composition of unbounded Hilbert-space domains has been formed.

Decomposition and harmonic representatives. For smooth $u$, [F1] gives $u=\Pi u+(I-\Pi)u=\Pi u+DD^*Gu+D^*DGu$, and the three summands are pairwise orthogonal: the harmonic summand is orthogonal to both images by step 3.1, and $(Da,D^*b)_{L^2}=(D^2a,b)_{L^2}=0$ since $D^2=0$. Conversely a harmonic form or a form in the image of $D$ or $D^*$ lies in the displayed ambient degree, so this is the orthogonal smooth decomposition. If $u$ is closed, $Du=0$, then step 4.1 gives $DGu=GDu=0$ and the coexact term vanishes: $u=\Pi u+D(D^*Gu)$, a harmonic representative of the class. If a harmonic $h$ is exact, $h=Dv$, then $\|h\|_2^2=(Dv,h)_{L^2}=(v,D^*h)_{L^2}=0$ because $D^*h=0$ by step 3.1, so $h=0$; hence $h\mapsto[h]$ is injective, and the preceding formula makes it surjective. It is linear as the composition of a linear projection with a linear quotient map, and its domain is finite dimensional by [F1]; the same argument applies over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$.

Conclusion and endpoints. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 verified the exact scalar-positive-symbol, formal-symmetry and nonnegativity hypotheses for the de Rham and Dolbeault Laplacians, so [F1] gives genuine nonnegative selfadjoint realizations with domain $H^2$, finite smooth kernels, smoothing projections and smooth Green inverses; steps 3.1 through 5.1 proved the degree, commutation, orthogonal-decomposition and harmonic-representative assertions for both complexes. At the endpoint degrees the operators mapping outside the displayed range are zero by the degree convention of [F3], so the identities hold there as well. The trivial line bundle case gives the usual Dolbeault cohomology of complex-valued forms, and no sheaf comparison has been used or asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold without boundary, of real dimension at least two. Its metric defines the $L^2$ pairing on forms by the Riemannian density; orientation is unnecessary. Let $d^*$ denote the formal adjoint of $d$, and $\Delta=dd^*+d^*d$ on total real forms, or on their complexification. With domain $H^2$ the operator is nonnegative and selfadjoint. Its degreewise smooth kernels $\mathcal H^k$ are finite dimensional, and there is an orthogonal smooth decomposition
$$\Omega^k(M)=\mathcal H^k\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}d\Omega^{k-1}(M)\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}d^*\Omega^{k+1}(M).$$
The map $h\mapsto[h]$ is an isomorphism $\mathcal H^k\to H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)$, over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ as appropriate.

More generally let $X$ be a compact complex manifold of complex dimension $m\ge1$ with a smooth Hermitian metric. Let $E$ be a holomorphic bundle of finite rank with a smooth Hermitian metric. The holomorphic bundle structure supplies frames with holomorphic invertible transition matrices; the Hermitian metric is separate smooth positive-definite pairing data. On $E$-valued $(p,q)$ forms, define $\bar\partial_E$ by the coefficientwise Dolbeault operator in holomorphic bundle charts and let $\bar\partial_E^*$ be its formal adjoint. For each fixed $p$, $\Delta_{\bar\partial_E}=\bar\partial_E\bar\partial_E^*+\bar\partial_E^*\bar\partial_E$ on the sum over $q$ is nonnegative and selfadjoint on $H^2$; its smooth harmonic spaces $\mathcal H_E^{p,q}$ are finite dimensional and
$$\Omega^{p,q}(X,E)=\mathcal H_E^{p,q}\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\bar\partial_E\Omega^{p,q-1}(X,E)\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\bar\partial_E^*\Omega^{p,q+1}(X,E).$$
In particular harmonic forms represent the smooth Dolbeault quotient
$$H_{\bar\partial}^{p,q}(X,E):=\ker\bar\partial_E/\operatorname{im}\bar\partial_E$$
uniquely. Terms outside the degree range are zero. This asserts smooth Dolbeault cohomology; an identification with sheaf cohomology requires a separate Dolbeault-resolution comparison theorem.

For either complex write $D=d$ or $D=\bar\partial_E$, $P=DD^*+D^*D$, and let $\Pi,G$ be the preceding Green projection and inverse. They preserve degree, $G$ preserves smooth forms, and on smooth forms
$$DG=GD,\qquad D^*G=GD^*,\qquad D\Pi=\Pi D=D^*\Pi=\Pi D^*=0.$$
Every closed smooth $u$ satisfies $u=\Pi u+D(D^*Gu)$.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb Z^n\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be the integer lattice acting
on $\mathbb R^n$ by translations, and let $T^n=\mathbb R^n/\mathbb Z^n$ carry
the quotient topology with quotient map $q:\mathbb R^n\to T^n$. Then:

1. there is a Riemannian metric $g$ on $T^n$, unique, with
   $q^*g=\sum_{i=1}^n dx^i\otimes dx^i$; with this metric $T^n$ is a
   connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold and $q$ is a surjective local
   isometry;
2. $(T^n,g)$ is geodesically and metrically complete, and for $n\ge2$ it has
   vanishing sectional curvature: $K=0$ on every tangent two-plane;
3. the quotient charts of the proof identify $T_{[x]}T^n$ with $\mathbb R^n$,
   and under that identification the maximal geodesic with initial datum
   $v\in\mathbb R^n$ is
   $$t\mapsto[x+tv],\qquad t\in\mathbb R,$$
   so that the exponential map is defined on all of $T_{[x]}T^n$ and
   $\exp_{[x]}(v)=[x+v]$; in particular $\exp_{[x]}$ is not injective, since
   $\exp_{[x]}(0)=\exp_{[x]}(e_1)=[x]$ for the nonzero lattice vector
   $e_1\in\mathbb Z^n$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $k\ge 0$. A **smooth differential $k$-form**
on $M$ is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M\to M$. The space of such forms
is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, and $\Omega^0(M)=C^\infty(M)$.

Let $X:M\to TM$ be a smooth section of the tangent bundle, that is, a smooth
vector field on $M$, and let $\omega\in\Omega^k(M)$. The **interior product**
$\iota_X\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$ is defined pointwise by

$$ (\iota_X\omega)_p:=\iota_{X_p}\omega_p. $$

For $k=0$, adopt the formal convention $\Omega^{-1}(M):=\{0\}$ and set
$\iota_X\omega:=0$.

This pointwise field is smooth. Indeed, in local coordinates write
$X=\sum_jX^j\partial_j$ and expand $\omega$ in the smooth frame $dx^I$ as in
[[prop-local-coordinate-expression-for-a-differential-form]]. The coefficients
of $\iota_X\omega$ are signed finite sums of products $X^j\omega_I$, and are
therefore smooth.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<n}[a_j,b_j]\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, where $n\ge1$ and every $a_j<b_j$. If $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, then for every permutation of the coordinates the corresponding repeated Riemann integral exists and equals $\int_Qf$.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

derivations.claim: Each class has a representative in $[0,1]^n$, by subtracting the integer parts of its coordinates. Thus $q([0,1]^n)=T^n$; pulling an open cover back to this compact cube and projecting a finite subcover proves compactness. The local coframes $dx^j$ agree across the translational changes of [F2], so they descend to a global orthonormal coframe, and its dual vector fields are the descended $\partial_j$. For a form $u$, its pullback is invariant under integer translations because $q(x+m)=q(x)$; therefore its coefficients in this coframe are smooth periodic functions.

Write $u=\sum_Iu_I dx^I$ in that coframe. The coordinate formula and [F1] give $d=\sum_j\varepsilon(dx^j)\partial_j$. Integrating each coefficient derivative over $[0,1]^n$ by [F3] cancels opposite-face terms by periodicity, so the formal adjoint identity gives $d^*=-\sum_j\iota_{\partial_j}\partial_j$. Here the density integral equals the cube integral: subdivide the cube into finitely many small boxes lying in quotient charts and use their Euclidean density; the shared faces have zero Riemann content. The wedge/contraction identity proved in [F1], $\varepsilon(dx^j)\iota_{\partial_l}+\iota_{\partial_l}\varepsilon(dx^j)=\delta_{jl}I$, now gives $\Delta u=-\sum_{I,j}\partial_j^2u_I dx^I$. One more integration by parts using [F3] gives $(\Delta u,u)_2=\sum_{I,j}\int_{[0,1]^n}|\partial_j u_I|^2$.

If $u$ is harmonic, the sum of nonnegative integrals in step 2.1 is zero. Each derivative is continuous, so a nonzero value would give a neighbourhood with positive integral; hence every $\partial_j u_I$ vanishes everywhere. Integration along line segments in $\mathbb R^n$ gives constant coefficients. Conversely constant coefficients give $\Delta u=0$ by step 2.1. The increasing wedge basis has $\binom nk$ members, and [F1] identifies this harmonic space with de Rham cohomology, proving the asserted representative and dimension claims.
